title: Connections
intro: Who taught whom, who was shaped by whom, and where authors in the archive argued with each other. Each link carries a short note on what it rests on. This is a first, partial map: it only joins authors who both have pages here.
source_note: compiled by the archive from the authors' biographies and standard reference works; corrections welcome at contact@islamicarchives.org

edges.note: Abduh was Afghani's closest disciple; they edited al-ʿUrwa al-wuthqā together in Paris in 1884.
Rida became Abduh's student and biographer, and put Abduh's Qurʾān lessons into Tafsīr al-Manār.
Hamka read the Cairo reformists through al-Manār; his Tafsīr al-Azhar draws on it.
Al-Banna read Rida's journal al-Manār as a young man and took its reformist programme into the Muslim Brotherhood.
Al-Qaradawi joined the Brotherhood as a student and counted al-Banna among his formative influences.
Tariq Ramadan is al-Banna's grandson and has written on his legacy.
Shibli taught at Sir Syed's Aligarh college, then broke with its modernist line and helped build the Nadwa alternative.
Iqbal's invitation brought Maududi to the Punjab in 1938, where he began building Jamaat-e-Islami.
Qutb took the language of divine sovereignty (ḥākimiyya) and jāhiliyya from Maududi's writings.
Islahi was among the founders of Jamaat-e-Islami and left it in 1958 over its direction.
Ghamidi studied under Islahi and carried his Qurʾānic-coherence method into his own work.
Ghamidi was a member of Jamaat-e-Islami until he left in the late 1970s.
Wahiduddin Khan was in the Jamaat and later wrote against Maududi's political reading of Islam.
Khurshid Ahmad worked with Maududi in Jamaat-e-Islami and later published his writings in English through the Islamic Foundation.
Brothers. Muhammad Qutb edited, defended and republished Sayyid's writings.
Al-Hawali wrote his Umm al-Qurā thesis under Muhammad Qutb's supervision.
Schuon corresponded with Guénon and began from his Traditionalist perspective, later founding his own order.
Lings went to Cairo in 1939, met Guénon, and worked as his secretary before following Schuon.
After Guénon's death in 1951 Lings became a close follower of Schuon.
Nasr's Traditionalism comes chiefly from Schuon, whose work he read as a student.
Dagli did his doctorate at George Washington University under Nasr.
Mutahhari studied under Khomeini in Qom and was among his closest allies.
Mutahhari attended Tabatabai's philosophy lessons in Qom.
Javadi Amoli studied philosophy and exegesis with Tabatabai.
Montazeri was Khomeini's student, and was later his designated successor until their break in 1989.
Mesbah Yazdi studied with Khomeini in Qom.
Mutahhari criticised Shariati's approach to religion and sociology in the early 1970s.
Gülen's movement grew out of the Nurcu circles that followed Nursi's Risale-i Nur.
Hamza Yusuf studied with Bin Bayyah and works with him on the Forum for Promoting Peace in Muslim Societies.
Co-founders of Zaytuna College in California.
Taqi Usmani called Abu Ghudda his teacher and wrote his obituary.
Abu Ghudda was a leading critic of al-Albani's independent hadith grading and his attitude to the madhhabs.
Brothers; both are sons of Mufti Muhammad Shafi.
Wadud's Qur'an and Woman builds on Rahman's method of reading the Qurʾān as a coherent ethical whole.
Both launched an 'Islamisation of knowledge' in the late 1970s: al-Attas through language and metaphysics, al-Faruqi through the IIIT's methods.
Ally has said that Deedat's lectures led him into the study of the Bible and comparative religion.
Brown's writing on hadith engages Azami's replies to Western scholarship on early hadith.
